title: Wikipedia Notability Requirements, Explained Without the Myths
metaDescription: What Wikipedia notability actually requires: significant coverage in reliable, independent sources — and which press clips do not count.
keywords: wikipedia notability requirements, general notability guideline, significant coverage wikipedia, independent sources wikipedia
excerpt: Notability is not fame, follower count, or a polished bio. It is a sourcing test. Here is how reviewers actually apply it.
body:
Most people who ask for a Wikipedia page start in the wrong place. They draft a biography, polish a company history, or gather testimonials. Reviewers start somewhere else: the sources.

Wikipedia’s general notability guideline asks a narrow question. Has the subject received significant coverage in reliable sources that are independent of the subject? Every word in that sentence does work. Skip any one of them and the draft usually fails, no matter how carefully it is written.

Significant coverage is not a mention

A name in a list, a quote in someone else’s profile, or a one-line award note is not enough. Significant coverage means the source spends real attention on the subject — typically multiple paragraphs that discuss who they are, what they did, or why it mattered.

Trade directories, conference speaker pages, and “top 40 under 40” roundups often look impressive in a pitch deck. On Wikipedia they rarely clear the bar unless the write-up itself is substantial and independent.

Independence rules out your own material

Your website, press releases, sponsored features, and company blogs do not establish notability. They can sometimes support basic facts later, but they do not prove the world has noticed the subject on its own terms. Wikipedia’s guidance on independent sources is blunt about this for a reason: the encyclopedia summarizes what others have already published, not what a subject wants published.

Reliability is about editorial control

Major newspapers, established magazines, academic presses, and serious trade journals with identifiable editors usually qualify. Personal blogs, social posts, most podcasts without strong editorial process, and user-edited sites usually do not. Borderline outlets exist; when they do, reviewers look at reputation, corrections policy, and whether the piece shows original reporting.

Subject-specific guidelines sit on top of the GNG

Academics, athletes, companies, and creative professionals have additional notability essays. Those guides refine the test. They do not replace the need for solid secondary coverage. A company that fails the general test will not be saved by a clever reading of the corporate notability page.

What a useful notability assessment looks like

Before anyone opens the editor, list the strongest independent pieces you can find. For each source, note the outlet, date, depth, and whether the subject is the focus. If you cannot name several substantial pieces, the honest answer is to wait — or to strengthen real-world coverage first — rather than force a draft into the review queue.

That early verdict is the difference between a durable article and months of declines. If you want a structured read on your own source pile, our Wikipedia page creation work begins with that assessment, not with a promise of publication.

title: How Long Does It Take to Create a Wikipedia Page?
metaTitle: How Long Does It Take to Create a Wikipedia Page?
metaDescription: Realistic timelines for Wikipedia page creation: research and drafting vs Articles for Creation review backlog, and what actually speeds things up.
keywords: how long wikipedia page creation, wikipedia articles for creation timeline, AfC backlog, wikipedia review time
excerpt: Drafting can take weeks. Volunteer review can take months. Here is what controls the clock — and what does not.
body:
Clients often ask for a date. Wikipedia does not work on delivery calendars the way a website launch does. The work splits into two clocks: the editorial clock you can manage, and the volunteer review clock you cannot.

The part you can plan: research and drafting

When the sources already exist, a careful draft usually takes a few weeks. That window covers source evaluation, outline, neutral writing, citation checking, and an internal review pass for promotional language. Thin sourcing stretches the timeline because the honest response is often “not yet,” not “write harder.”

Rushing this stage is a false economy. A weak draft that enters review early tends to come back declined, then waits again after revision.

The part you cannot control: Articles for Creation

Most new accounts and many paid contributors use the Articles for Creation process. Drafts sit in a queue reviewed by volunteers. Waiting periods of several months are common when the backlog is large, and submissions are not guaranteed to be reviewed in neat chronological order.

Nobody can sell a guaranteed early review. Offers that claim otherwise are either misleading or violating community norms.

What actually improves the odds

  • Clear notability on the page. Reviewers should see independent secondary sources without hunting.
  • Neutral tone. Adjectives that sell trigger declines faster than almost anything else.
  • Complete citations. Dead links, missing publishers, and mismatched claims burn time.
  • Continued polishing after submission. A pending draft can still be improved while it waits.

After acceptance

Publication is not the finish line. Early weeks matter: watchlist monitoring, talk-page questions, and routine cleanup. That is why many engagements include a short stabilisation period after the move to article space.

If you need a realistic estimate for a specific subject, start with source strength. Our process page walks through the five stages we use before anyone talks about submission timing: our editorial process.

title: Paid Wikipedia Editing: Disclosure, COI, and What Gets People Banned
metaTitle: Paid Wikipedia Editing Disclosure & COI Rules Explained
metaDescription: How paid Wikipedia editing must be disclosed under Wikimedia Terms of Use, what conflict of interest means in practice, and why secrecy backfires.
keywords: paid wikipedia editing disclosure, wikipedia conflict of interest, WP:PAID, wikipedia COI guidelines
excerpt: Paid editing is allowed when it is disclosed. Undisclosed advocacy is what burns accounts, agencies, and sometimes the client’s reputation too.
body:
People hear “paid editing” and assume the practice itself is forbidden. That is not what the rules say. The hard line is secrecy. Wikimedia’s Terms of Use require paid contributors to disclose employer, client, and affiliation. English Wikipedia’s conflict-of-interest guidance builds on that requirement.

What disclosure looks like in practice

Paid editors are expected to declare the relationship on their user page, on relevant article talk pages, and in edit summaries where paid work happens. Templates such as connected-contributor notices exist so other editors can see the relationship without guessing.

If your agency refuses to disclose, that is not a clever workaround. It is a Terms of Use problem waiting to surface — often publicly.

Conflict of interest is about incentives, not just paycheques

A company’s founder, a PR lead, or a subject’s family member has a conflict even when no invoice is involved. The recommended path is the same: propose changes on the talk page with sources, rather than rewriting the article in promotional voice. Living-person policy still allows obvious error fixes, but “obvious” is narrower than most subjects hope.

Why undisclosed advocacy keeps making headlines

When sockpuppets or undeclared paid accounts are uncovered, the cleanup is rarely quiet. Blocks follow. Articles get scrutinised. Clients sometimes receive press coverage they never wanted. The Wikimedia Foundation has been clear for years that paying someone who will not disclose is a bad bargain.

What ethical paid work still cannot do

  • Guarantee acceptance or permanent protection from deletion.
  • Remove well-sourced critical material because it is inconvenient.
  • Insert claims that independent sources do not support.
  • Buy a favourable review in the AfC queue.

A practical client checklist

Ask any firm three questions before you hire them: Will you disclose? Will you show the sources that establish notability before drafting? Will you refuse work that requires promotional framing? If the answers are soft, keep looking.

We treat disclosure as non-negotiable in page editing and creation work. Transparency is slower than stealth. It is also the only approach that survives contact with experienced reviewers.

title: Why Wikipedia Pages Get Deleted (And How to Avoid the Usual Traps)
metaTitle: Why Wikipedia Pages Get Deleted — Common Causes
metaDescription: The most common reasons Wikipedia articles and drafts are deleted or declined: weak notability, promotional tone, COI issues, and thin sourcing.
keywords: why wikipedia pages get deleted, wikipedia article deletion, promotional wikipedia page, AfC declined
excerpt: Deletion is rarely mysterious. Most failed pages share the same handful of problems — and they are visible before the first draft is filed.
body:
When a page disappears, subjects often assume politics or sabotage. Sometimes disputes are real. Far more often, the article never met the bar that Wikipedia uses for every other topic.

1. Notability was assumed, not evidenced

Awards, revenue, follower counts, and “first in the region” claims do not substitute for independent secondary coverage. If the best sources are press releases and partner blogs, deletion discussions tend to end quickly.

2. The tone reads like a brochure

Words such as leading, visionary, renowned, and cutting-edge are red flags unless an independent source used them and you are attributing that source. Wikipedia summarises; it does not endorse. Promotional voice is one of the fastest paths to a decline at Articles for Creation and to maintenance tags after publication.

3. Citations do not match the claims

A dense reference list impresses nobody if the links are dead, point to unrelated pages, or support only a fraction of what the prose asserts. Reviewers check. So do deletion nominators.

4. Conflict of interest was handled badly

Undeclared paid editing, sockpuppets, and aggressive self-editing invite scrutiny that ordinary weak drafts do not. Even a salvageable topic can be damaged by the account history attached to it.

5. The subject was notable once, then the sourcing aged out

Long-standing articles can still face challenges if coverage was always thin or if the page drifted into original research and résumé padding. Maintenance is not optional for subjects who remain in public view.

Prevention beats recovery

The cheapest fix is the earliest one: a sober source audit before drafting. If publication already happened and the page is unstable, the work shifts to sourcing, neutrality, and talk-page process rather than quiet rewrites.

For subjects dealing with tags, disputes, or reputation-sensitive coverage, see our notes on reputation and entity work — still within policy, still disclosed.

title: Reliable Sources for Wikipedia: What Counts and What Never Will
metaTitle: Reliable Sources for Wikipedia Articles (Practical Guide)
metaDescription: A practical guide to Wikipedia reliable sources: newspapers, journals, and books that help — plus press releases, blogs, and directories that do not.
keywords: reliable sources wikipedia, wikipedia citations, press release wikipedia, secondary sources wikipedia
excerpt: Not every link with a logo is a usable source. This is the sorting method we use before a single sentence gets drafted.
body:
Wikipedia’s content policies rest on three pillars that keep colliding in client conversations: verifiability, no original research, and neutral point of view. All three depend on sources. Get the sources wrong and elegant prose will not save the page.

Secondary sources do the heavy lifting

Secondary sources analyse, summarise, or contextualise a topic. A newspaper profile, a scholarly overview, or a serious magazine feature usually sits in this category. Primary sources — filings, interviews, the subject’s own site — can support uncontroversial facts, but they rarely establish notability on their own.

A working hierarchy for most biographies and companies

  • Usually strong: major newspapers, established magazines, academic journals, books from recognised publishers, serious trade press with editorial staff.
  • Handle carefully: local outlets with uneven standards, industry blogs with light editing, interview pieces that mostly quote the subject.
  • Usually weak for notability: press releases, wire reprints of releases, company blogs, sponsored “newsroom” features, most social media, crowdfunding pages, Wikipedia mirrors.

Independence is easy to misunderstand

A glowing article still fails the independence test if the subject paid for it, dictated it, or published it. Wikipedia’s pages on reliable sources and independent sources are worth reading in full before you build a citation list around marketing assets.

How we stress-test a source pile

For each candidate piece, ask: Who wrote it? Who edited it? Was the subject the focus? Does the outlet correct errors? Is there a financial relationship? If you cannot answer those questions, do not hang an article on that link.

Good research is slower than dumping every Google result into a draft. It is also the only way Wikipedia content writing stays stable after publication.

title: How to Improve an Existing Wikipedia Page Without Making It Worse
metaTitle: How to Improve an Existing Wikipedia Page (Policy-Safe)
metaDescription: How to fix tags, sourcing gaps, and outdated sections on an existing Wikipedia article — using talk-page process and reliable sources.
keywords: improve wikipedia page, edit existing wikipedia article, wikipedia maintenance tags, wikipedia talk page edit request
excerpt: Existing articles fail in quieter ways: tags, dead links, promotional drift, and missing milestones. Here is a repair order that respects the rules.
body:
Improving a live article is different from creating one. The page already has watchers, history, and expectations. Large unexplained rewrites — especially by new or undeclared accounts — draw attention fast.

Start with a diagnosis, not a redesign

Read the talk page, the page history, and every maintenance tag at the top. Tags are not decoration. Each one points to a specific problem: tone, sourcing, autobiography, notability, or outdated information. Fix the cause; do not delete the banner and hope nobody notices.

A practical repair order

  1. Correct clear factual errors with citations already accepted on similar articles.
  2. Replace dead or weak references before expanding new sections.
  3. Trim promotional language even when the subject dislikes a flatter tone.
  4. Add milestones only when independent sources cover them — not because the subject announced them.
  5. Leave disputed or sensitive biography material to careful, well-sourced edits that follow living-person policy.

When you have a conflict of interest

Do not “quietly improve” your own article. Disclose and use the talk page. Edit requests that arrive with proposed text and reliable sources are far more likely to be taken seriously than vague complaints that the page is unfair.

What ongoing management is for

Public subjects attract drive-by edits, vandalism, and well-meant but unsourced additions. A watchlist routine catches problems while they are small. Waiting six months turns a one-line fix into a sourcing project.

If you need a structured audit of an existing article, our editing service and page management work both start from the live page as it stands — tags, history, and all — not from a marketing brief.

title: Can I Pay Someone to Write My Wikipedia Page?
metaTitle: Can I Pay Someone to Write My Wikipedia Page? (Honest Answer)
metaDescription: Yes — paid Wikipedia writing is allowed with disclosure. Here is what you can buy, what you cannot, and how to vet an agency.
keywords: can i pay someone to write my wikipedia page, hire wikipedia writer, paid wikipedia page creation
excerpt: Paying for drafting is legal when disclosed. Paying for a guaranteed outcome is a fiction. Here is the difference.
body:
Short answer: yes, you can pay a professional to research and draft a Wikipedia article — provided the relationship is disclosed and the subject already meets notability. You cannot pay anyone for a guaranteed acceptance, a locked article, or a rewrite that invents coverage that does not exist.

What payment actually buys

A competent firm sells labour: source auditing, neutral drafting, citation work, disclosure, and responses to reviewer comments. The encyclopedia’s volunteer reviewers still decide whether the draft meets the guidelines. That split is why ethical agencies talk about probability and preparation, not promises.

What to ask before you hire

  • Will you disclose paid contributions on-wiki?
  • Will you show a written notability verdict before drafting?
  • What happens if the sources are too thin — do you stop, or do you invent a pitch?
  • Are pricing and revision scope written down?

Red flags

“Guaranteed approval,” “rejection-free,” undeclared accounts, and agencies that refuse to discuss Wikimedia’s Terms of Use are not shortcuts. They are liabilities. When undeclared paid editing is uncovered, the cleanup is public and often worse than never filing.

A sane sequence

Start with a notability assessment. If the sources support an article, move to creation with disclosure. If they do not, invest in earning independent coverage in the real world first — not in a draft that will be declined.

For costs, see our published Wikipedia page cost tiers. For the disclosure rules in depth, read paid editing and COI.

title: How to Get a Wikipedia Page for Yourself (Without Getting Declined)
metaTitle: How to Get a Wikipedia Page for Yourself — Step by Step
metaDescription: A practical path to a Wikipedia article about yourself: source audit first, conflict-of-interest rules, and when to hire a disclosed editor.
keywords: how to get a wikipedia page for yourself, create wikipedia page about myself, wikipedia autobiography
excerpt: Autobiography is the hardest path on Wikipedia. Here is the sequence that actually works — and the shortcuts that fail.
body:
People search “how to get a Wikipedia page for yourself” expecting a form. There isn’t one. There is a sourcing test, a conflict-of-interest problem, and a review queue staffed by volunteers who have seen every promotional trick.

Step 1: Prove coverage exists without you

List independent articles, books, or journal pieces that discuss you in depth. Press releases, your site, and sponsored features do not count toward notability. If the list is empty, stop. Earn coverage first.

Step 2: Do not write the article as autobiography

Subjects and their staff have a conflict of interest. Drafting your own page in promotional voice is the classic decline pattern. Propose sourced text on the talk page, or hire a disclosed editor who will write from the sources — including unflattering ones.

Step 3: Expect neutrality, not brand control

A Wikipedia article summarises what reliable sources published. You do not get veto power over well-sourced criticism. Attempts to scrub inconvenient facts usually attract more scrutiny.

Step 4: Disclose paid help

If someone is paid to draft or edit, that relationship must be declared. Secrecy is the policy violation, not the invoice.

When a free assessment helps

If you are unsure whether the sources clear the bar, request a notability assessment before commissioning a full draft. For the guideline itself, see our longer explainer on notability requirements.

title: What Drives Wikipedia Page Creation Cost (Beyond the Sticker Price)
metaTitle: Wikipedia Page Creation Cost Factors Explained
metaDescription: Why Wikipedia page creation pricing varies: source volume, prior rejections, dual review, and monitoring — not fake approval guarantees.
keywords: wikipedia page creation cost, wikipedia page price factors, cost of wikipedia page
excerpt: Price follows research load and risk — not how badly someone wants a page. Here is what actually moves the quote.
body:
Clients comparing agencies often see wild price spreads. The honest drivers are boring: how many sources must be read and graded, whether a prior rejection must be unwound, how much dual review the draft needs, and whether monitoring after publication is included.

Source volume raises cost even when the article stays short

A heavily covered subject can cost more than a lightly covered one. Forty independent pieces must be reconciled; contradictions take time. Thin subjects are cheaper only when you stop at “not yet” instead of forcing a draft.

Prior declines add forensic work

Reading reviewer comments, auditing what failed, and deciding whether coverage has improved since is a separate labour block. Agencies that ignore the decline history tend to repeat it.

What should never be a line item

Guaranteed acceptance, guaranteed ranking, and guaranteed knowledge panels are not deliverables anyone controls. If they appear on an invoice, treat the rest of the pitch with suspicion.

Published tiers beat opaque “custom only” quotes

We publish starting points from $700 upward and fix the figure in writing after assessment. Full package detail lives on the pricing page. Creation scope is described under page creation.

title: Wikipedia Articles for Creation: What to Expect in the Queue
metaTitle: Wikipedia Articles for Creation (AfC) — What to Expect
metaDescription: How Wikipedia’s Articles for Creation process works, why waits run long, and how to prepare a draft that reviewers can assess quickly.
keywords: wikipedia articles for creation, AfC wikipedia, wikipedia draft review process
excerpt: AfC is a volunteer queue, not a customer-support ticket. Here is what that means for timelines and preparation.
body:
Articles for Creation (AfC) lets drafts be reviewed before they enter main article space. For many new or paid contributors it is the responsible path. It is also where patience gets tested.

Reviewers are volunteers

There is no paid SLA. Backlogs stretch. Order is not strictly first-in, first-out. A clear, well-sourced draft still waits — but a muddy promotional draft waits, then declines, then waits again after revision.

What reviewers look for first

  • Independent secondary sources visible without archaeology
  • Neutral tone and proportionate structure
  • Citations that actually support the sentences above them
  • Honest handling of living-person and COI issues

What you can do while a draft waits

Keep improving citations, trimming hype, and watching for new independent coverage. Do not open parallel copies under new accounts to “speed things up.” That pattern is noticed.

After acceptance

Mainspace is not a finish line. Early edits, tags, and talk-page questions are common. Plan for monitoring through stabilisation. For timeline context, see how long creation takes.

title: Wikipedia vs Google Knowledge Panel: What Each One Is For
metaTitle: Wikipedia vs Google Knowledge Panel — Differences Explained
metaDescription: How Wikipedia articles and Google knowledge panels relate, why neither is guaranteed from the other, and what entity work can realistically improve.
keywords: wikipedia vs google knowledge panel, get google knowledge panel, wikipedia knowledge panel
excerpt: A Wikipedia page helps entity clarity. It does not flip a switch that forces a Google panel.
body:
Clients often hire for “a Wikipedia page so we get a knowledge panel.” Those are related signals, not a package deal. Wikipedia is a volunteer-edited encyclopedia. A Google knowledge panel is assembled by Google from many public sources when Google decides the entity is clear enough to show.

What Wikipedia contributes

A well-sourced article and Wikidata item give search and answer systems a consistent factual record. That can help entity resolution. It does not obligate Google to display a panel, nor to show the facts in the order a brand prefers.

What actually improves panel odds

Consistent legal names, dates, and identifiers across Wikipedia, Wikidata, official sites, and other structured databases. Contradictions confuse machines. Guaranteed-panel vendors skip this honesty.

What to commission

If you need an encyclopedia article, start with notability and creation. If you already have an article and conflicting entity records, look at knowledge-panel / entity work and reputation & entity building. Neither service sells a switch Google alone controls.

title: Why Wikipedia Page Monitoring Matters After Publication
metaTitle: Wikipedia Page Monitoring After Publication — Why It Matters
metaDescription: Why published Wikipedia articles need monitoring: vandalism, unsourced edits, tags, and how watchlist triage differs from full page management.
keywords: wikipedia page monitoring, monitor wikipedia page, wikipedia vandalism watch
excerpt: Publication is when strangers can edit your article. Monitoring is how you notice before a wrong fact travels.
body:
Once an article is live, anyone can change it. Most edits are fine. Some introduce errors, promotional language, or vandalism. Unwatched pages can carry a wrong figure for months — long enough to be copied into press and AI answers.

Monitoring vs full management

Monitoring is detection and triage: watchlist coverage, classifying edits, escalating contested changes. Full page management adds scheduled updates, dead-link repair, and deeper accuracy reviews. Many subjects start with monitoring alone.

What you cannot buy

You cannot lock the article for a client. Temporary protection is an administrator decision during sustained vandalism, granted on Wikipedia’s terms.

A practical habit

Agree a review cycle, escalate urgent categories quickly, and keep an edit log. Catching a problem the same week is cheap; catching it after syndication is not. For repair patterns on live pages, see improving an existing page.

title: Am I Notable Enough for Wikipedia? A Self-Check That Isn’t Wishful
metaTitle: Am I Notable Enough for Wikipedia? Self-Check Guide
metaDescription: A blunt self-check for Wikipedia notability: significant independent coverage vs awards, revenue, and follower counts that do not substitute.
keywords: am i notable enough for wikipedia, wikipedia notability self check, wikipedia eligibility test
excerpt: Fame is the wrong metric. Coverage is the right one. Use this checklist before you spend on a draft.
body:
“Am I notable enough?” is the right question asked the wrong way. Wikipedia does not score celebrity. It looks for significant coverage in multiple reliable sources independent of you.

Self-check

  1. Can you name three independent pieces that discuss you (or your company) in depth — not just mention you?
  2. Were those pieces edited by outlets with a reputation for fact-checking?
  3. Did you pay for, dictate, or publish those pieces yourself?
  4. If you removed your website and press kit from the internet, would the remaining coverage still tell a coherent story?

If you fail any of those, a draft is premature.

What does not substitute for coverage

Revenue, headcount, follower counts, awards alone, “first in the city” claims, and partner testimonials. They may be true. They are not the notability test.

Get a second opinion without buying a draft

Commission a notability assessment — or start with our free screen via contact. Read the fuller policy walkthrough in notability requirements explained.

title: Why Press Releases and Sponsored Content Fail Wikipedia Notability
metaTitle: Press Releases & Sponsored Content on Wikipedia — Why They Fail
metaDescription: Why Wikipedia rejects press releases, sponsored features, and company blogs as notability evidence — and what independent coverage looks like instead.
keywords: press release wikipedia, sponsored content wikipedia, company blog wikipedia notability
excerpt: Marketing assets are useful for dates and spellings. They are useless for proving the world noticed you independently.
body:
Communications teams arrive with binders of “coverage” that turn out to be wire reprints of releases, sponsored native ads, and partner blogs. Those assets help orientation. They do not establish notability.

Independence is the missing ingredient

Wikipedia needs sources that are independent of the subject. If the subject paid for the piece, supplied the copy, or published it, the piece fails that test even when the layout looks like news.

How to tell sponsored from reported

  • Labelled “sponsored,” “partner,” “brand story,” or “paid content”
  • No identifiable journalist beyond a company spokesperson
  • Identical wording to a press release
  • Outlet known for pay-to-play features

What to gather instead

Unpaid profiles, investigative or analytical pieces, book chapters, peer-reviewed work, and serious trade reporting where an editor — not a client — controlled the story. Our reliable sources guide and research service start from that sorting method.
